examShortTricks: Trick 1: Definitions in one line each — ore: mineral from which metal is extracted profitably; gangue/matrix: unwanted rocky impurity; flux: substance added to remove gangue; slag: fusible product of flux + gangue.
Trick 2: Slag equation: CaO (flux, basic) + SiO2 (gangue, acidic) → CaSiO3 (slag) — write it; it links all four definitions in one line.
Trick 3: Alloy vs amalgam: amalgam is an alloy containing MERCURY (Na–Hg, Zn–Hg); examples of alloys: brass (Cu+Zn), bronze (Cu+Sn).
keyPoints: Ore: naturally occurring mineral from which a metal can be extracted economically.
Gangue (matrix): earthy impurities associated with the ore.
Flux combines with gangue to form fusible slag.
Amalgam: alloy of a metal with mercury.
practiceQuestions: Q. Define flux and slag with one equation. (2 marks) — CaO + SiO2 → CaSiO3.
Q. What is an amalgam? Give one example. (1 mark) — alloy with mercury, e.g. sodium amalgam.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Flow order: concentration (removal of gangue) → calcination (carbonate/hydroxide ores, heated WITHOUT air) → roasting (sulphide ores, heated WITH air) → reduction (smelting/electrolysis) → refining.
Trick 2: Calcination vs roasting in one line: calcination = carbonate ore + no air (ZnCO3 → ZnO + CO2); roasting = sulphide ore + excess air (2ZnS + 3O2 → 2ZnO + 2SO2).
Trick 3: Carbon reduction vs electrolytic reduction: metals ABOVE Zn in activity series (Al, Na, Ca) need electrolysis; below Zn use carbon/CO reduction.
Trick 4: Thermite process for Cr/Mn: Al is the reducing agent (Al + metal oxide → Al2O3 + metal + heat).
keyPoints: Concentration removes gangue by gravity, froth floatation, magnetic or leaching methods.
Calcination: heating ore without air (carbonates/hydroxides).
Roasting: heating sulphide ore in excess air.
Reduction: carbon, CO, Al (thermite) or electrolysis; then refining.
practiceQuestions: Q. Differentiate calcination and roasting with one equation each. (3 marks) — as above (ZnCO3 vs ZnS).
Q. Why is aluminium extracted by electrolysis, not carbon reduction? (1 mark) — Al is too strong a reductant; carbon cannot reduce Al2O3 economically.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Poling = stirring molten impure metal with green wood poles: hydrocarbon gases REDUCE the oxide impurities (Cu2O + C/H2 → Cu) — 'green poles' is the keyword.
Trick 2: Electro-refinement: impure metal = anode, pure = cathode, metal salt solution = electrolyte; impurities fall as anode mud — give Cu refining with CuSO4.
Trick 3: Name other methods for one extra mark: distillation (Zn, Hg), liquation (Sn, Pb), vapour phase (Ni carbonyl).
keyPoints: Poling: volatile impurities of oxidised metals are reduced by wood gases.
Electro-refinement: anode dissolves, pure metal deposits on cathode; impurities collect as anode mud.
Other methods: distillation, liquation, zone refining, vapour-phase refining.
practiceQuestions: Q. What is poling and where is it used? (2 marks) — reduction of oxidised impurities in molten Cu using green wood poles.
Q. In copper electro-refining, what is the anode mud? (1 mark) — insoluble impurities (Au, Ag, Pt) settling below the anode.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Precipitation set: NaOH + metal salt solutions give coloured hydroxides — Fe3+ brown, Cu2+ pale blue, Zn2+/Al3+ white (dissolve in excess NaOH — amphoteric).
Trick 2: With CO: NaOH + CO → HCOONa (sodium formate) under pressure — the unusual 1-marker.
Trick 3: Uses list: soap manufacture, paper, refining petroleum, textile (mercerisation), lab reagent for CO2 absorption.
keyPoints: NaOH is a strong deliquescent alkali, soluble in water with heat evolution.
Precipitates metal hydroxides; Zn(OH)2 and Al(OH)3 dissolve in excess (amphoteric).
Absorbs CO2 and CO (sodium formate under pressure).
Used in soap, paper, textile and petroleum industries.
practiceQuestions: Q. What happens when excess NaOH is added to ZnSO4 solution? (2 marks) — white Zn(OH)2 first, then dissolves to sodium zincate Na2[Zn(OH)4].
Q. Give two uses of NaOH. (1 mark) — soap making, paper industry.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Hydrolysis one-liner: aqueous Na2CO3 is alkaline (CO3²− + H2O ⇌ HCO3− + OH−) — explains why it cleans grease.
Trick 2: With CO2: Na2CO3 + CO2 + H2O → 2NaHCO3 (sodium bicarbonate); with SO2: Na2SO3 + CO2 + H2O — same pattern, swap the acid gas.
Trick 3: Precipitation: CaCl2 + Na2CO3 → CaCO3↓ (white) + 2NaCl; Mg2+ similarly — hard-water softening application.
Trick 4: Heating test: 2NaHCO3 → Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2 — used to distinguish the two salts.
keyPoints: Na2CO3 (washing soda, Na2CO3·10H2O) is alkaline by hydrolysis.
Absorbs CO2 to form bicarbonate; precipitates Ca2+/Mg2+ carbonates.
Decomposes on strong heating only via the bicarbonate stage.
Uses: glass, soap, water softening, cleaning agent.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why is Na2CO3 solution alkaline? (2 marks) — carbonate hydrolysis produces OH− ions.
Q. Write the reaction of Na2CO3 with CO2. (1 mark) — Na2CO3 + CO2 + H2O → 2NaHCO3.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Formula table to memorise — quick lime CaO; bleaching powder Ca(OCl)Cl (CaOCl2); magnesia MgO; plaster of Paris CaSO4·½H2O; Epsom salt MgSO4·7H2O.
Trick 2: Plaster of Paris sets by hydration: CaSO4·½H2O + 1½H2O → CaSO4·2H2O (gypsum) — the setting equation is the standard 2-marker.
Trick 3: Bleaching powder release: Ca(OCl)Cl + dilute acid → Cl2 (available chlorine) — quote for its disinfectant use.
keyPoints: Quick lime CaO — made by heating limestone; used in cement and soil treatment.
Bleaching powder CaOCl2 — bleaching and disinfecting, releases chlorine.
Plaster of Paris CaSO4·½H2O — casts and casts for fractures; sets to gypsum.
Epsom salt MgSO4·7H2O — laxative; magnesia MgO — refractory lining, antacid.
practiceQuestions: Q. Write the molecular formula of plaster of Paris and its setting reaction. (2 marks) — CaSO4·½H2O; hydration to gypsum CaSO4·2H2O.
Q. Why is bleaching powder used for water purification? (1 mark) — liberates chlorine that kills germs.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Three trend lines — hydroxides: solubility INCREASES down (Be(OH)2 insoluble → Ba(OH)2 most); carbonates: all INSOLUBLE, decrease slightly; sulphates: DECREASE down (BaSO4 most insoluble).
Trick 2: Explain by hydration vs lattice energy: for hydroxides hydration energy wins as size grows; for sulphates lattice energy wins — that contrast earns the explanation mark.
Trick 3: Application: BaSO4 insolubility → barium meal X-ray; MgSO4 soluble → Epsom salt.
keyPoints: Hydroxide solubility increases from Be to Ba.
Sulphate solubility decreases from Be to Ba (BaSO4 insoluble).
Carbonates are insoluble; solubility decreases slightly down the group.
Trend decided by the competition between hydration and lattice energies.
practiceQuestions: Q. Arrange MgSO4, CaSO4, SrSO4, BaSO4 in decreasing solubility. (1 mark) — MgSO4 > CaSO4 > SrSO4 > BaSO4.
Q. Why is BaSO4 used in X-ray diagnosis? (1 mark) — highly insoluble and opaque to X-rays, non-toxic.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Thermal stability of carbonates and nitrates INCREASES down the group (Be/Mg decompose easily, Ba needs strong heat) — opposite of solubility trend for hydroxides.
Trick 2: Explanation: smaller cations polarise the carbonate/nitrate anion more (higher polarising power) → easier decomposition; bigger cations stabilise the anion.
Trick 3: Decomposition products: MCO3 → MO + CO2; nitrates of Be/Mg → NO2 + O2 + MO, heavier ones (Sr/Ba) → nitrite + O2 only.
keyPoints: Carbonate stability increases down group 2: BeCO3 < MgCO3 < CaCO3 < SrCO3 < BaCO3.
Nitrates follow the same stability order.
Polarising power of the cation decreases as ionic size increases.
Be and Mg nitrates give NO2; Sr/Ba nitrates give nitrites.
practiceQuestions: Q. Arrange the group-2 carbonates by thermal stability and explain. (3 marks) — BeCO3 least stable → BaCO3 most; polarisation argument.
Q. Products of heating Mg(NO3)2? (1 mark) — MgO + NO2 + O2.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Split by amount — macronutrients (needed >1 mg/g dry matter... quote C, H, O, N, P, K, Ca, Mg, S); micronutrients/trace (Fe, Mn, Zn, Cu, B, Mo, Cl).
Trick 2: Function pair for 2 marks: N — proteins/amino acids; P — ATP/nucleic acids; K — enzyme activation; Fe — haemoglobin/chlorophyll synthesis; Mg — chlorophyll central atom.
Trick 3: Deficiency symptoms score: N — chlorosis; P — poor root growth; Fe — interveinal chlorosis in young leaves.
keyPoints: Macronutrients: C, H, O, N, P, K, Ca, Mg, S — needed in large amounts.
Micronutrients: Fe, Mn, Zn, Cu, B, Mo, Cl — needed in trace amounts.
Mg is the central atom of chlorophyll; Fe is central to haemoglobin.
Deficiency causes chlorosis, necrosis and stunted growth.
practiceQuestions: Q. List four macronutrients and their one function. (2 marks) — N (protein), P (ATP/DNA), K (enzyme activation), Ca (cell wall/bone).
Q. Why is Mg a micronutrient for animals but macronutrient for plants? (1 mark) — plants need large Mg for chlorophyll; animals need only traces.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Na+/K+ pump stoichiometry: 3 Na+ OUT, 2 K+ IN per ATP — the ratio is the most-asked detail; driven by Na+/K+ ATPase.
Trick 2: Consequences: maintains resting membrane potential, cell volume and nerve impulse transmission — three outcomes for the 2-mark answer.
Trick 3: Na–glucose pump: Na+ gradient (secondary active transport) drags glucose INTO the cell against its gradient in the intestine — 'secondary transport' is the keyword.
keyPoints: Na+/K+ pump exports 3 Na+ and imports 2 K+ per ATP hydrolysed.
Maintains membrane potential, osmotic balance and nerve conduction.
Na–glucose co-transport uses the Na+ gradient to absorb glucose in the intestine.
Both are active transport mechanisms requiring energy.
practiceQuestions: Q. State the ion ratio of the Na+/K+ pump and its energy source. (2 marks) — 3 Na+ out : 2 K+ in; ATP via Na+/K+ ATPase.
Q. How is glucose absorbed in the intestine against its gradient? (2 marks) — Na–glucose symport driven by the Na+ electrochemical gradient.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: One effect each — Fe overload: haemochromatosis/liver damage; As: blackfoot disease, skin cancer; Hg (methylmercury): Minamata nerve disease; Pb: plumbism, brain/kidney damage, IQ loss in children; Cd: itai-itai bone disease, kidney failure.
Trick 2: Source column for the table: Fe — supplements/haemolysis; As — groundwater/pesticides; Hg — industrial effluent/fish; Pb — paint/petrol/pipes; Cd — batteries/zinc smelting.
Trick 3: Chelation therapy is the treatment line: EDTA/BAL bind the metal for excretion — quote for the remedy mark.
keyPoints: Heavy metals accumulate in tissues and block enzyme –SH groups.
Hg poisoning: Minamata disease from methylmercury in fish.
Cd poisoning: itai-itai disease and kidney damage.
Pb poisoning damages the nervous system, especially in children.
Treated by chelating agents (EDTA, BAL, DMSA).
practiceQuestions: Q. Name the disease caused by mercury and cadmium poisoning. (2 marks) — Minamata; itai-itai.
Q. How are heavy-metal poisonings treated? (1 mark) — chelation therapy with EDTA/BAL.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Alkyl group = alkane minus one H, general CnH2n+1 (methyl CH3–, ethyl C2H5–); functional group = the reactive atom/group (–OH, –CHO, –COOH, –X).
Trick 2: Homologous series definition in one line: compounds with the SAME general formula, same functional group, successive members differ by CH2 (14 u).
Trick 3: Exam pattern: 'give the general formula' — alkanes CnH2n+2, alkenes CnH2n, alkynes CnH2n−2, alcohols CnH2n+1OH.
keyPoints: Alkyl group: monovalent radical from an alkane, CnH2n+1.
Functional group: atom/group responsible for the characteristic reactions.
Homologous series: same general formula and functional group, successive members differ by –CH2–.
Properties change gradually along a homologous series.
practiceQuestions: Q. Define homologous series with one example. (2 marks) — CH4, C2H6, C3H8… differ by CH2, general CnH2n+2.
Q. Write the general formula of alkyl groups. (1 mark) — CnH2n+1.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Five types with one example each — chain (butane/isobutane), position (1- vs 2-chloropropane), functional (ethanol/dimethyl ether), metamerism (diethyl vs methyl ethyl ether), tautomerism (keto–enol).

Trick 2: Quick test order: same molecular formula? → same carbon skeleton? (chain) → same group position? (position) → same functional group? (functional) → different alkyl groups around a divalent group? (metamerism).
Trick 3: Metamerism needs a divalent atom/group (O, S, N) with two alkyl parts — C4H10O ethers show both chain and metamerism.
keyPoints: Chain (skeleton) isomerism: different carbon-chain arrangement.
Position isomerism: same group, different position.
Functional isomerism: same formula, different functional groups.
Metamerism: different alkyl groups attached to the same polyvalent group.
Tautomerism: dynamic keto–enol equilibrium.
practiceQuestions: Q. Show chain and position isomerism in C4H10/C4H9Cl. (2 marks) — n-butane vs isobutane; 1-chlorobutane vs 2-chlorobutane.
Q. Ethanol and dimethyl ether illustrate which isomerism? (1 mark) — functional isomerism.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: One-line trio — electrophile: electron-LOVING, accepts a pair (H+, NO2+, BF3, carbocation); nucleophile: electron-LOVING... donates a pair (OH−, CN−, NH3, carbanion); free radical: neutral with an unpaired electron (Cl·).
Trick 2: Charge test: electrophiles may be positive OR neutral (BF3, AlCl3); nucleophiles negative OR neutral (H2O, NH3) — 'charge is not the definition, electron pair behaviour is'.
Trick 3: Reaction mapping: substitution of benzene = electrophilic; hydrolysis of alkyl halide = nucleophilic; halogenation of methane in light = free-radical chain.
keyPoints: Electrophile: electron-pair acceptor (positive or neutral, e.g. H+, NO2+, BF3).
Nucleophile: electron-pair donor (negative or neutral, e.g. OH−, CN−, NH3).
Free radical: neutral species with one unpaired electron; formed by homolysis.
Each drives a different reaction mechanism class.
practiceQuestions: Q. Classify: BF3, OH−, Cl·, NH3. (2 marks) — electrophile; nucleophile; free radical; nucleophile.
Q. Which species attacks benzene in nitration? (1 mark) — nitronium ion NO2+, an electrophile.
